before.label: Political history
before.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

before.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
before.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Reinhart Koselleck, Vergangene Zukunft (1979), translated as Futures Past (1985; Columbia edition 2004). The German conceptual-history tradition is related to, but not a branch of, Skinner and Pocock’s Cambridge School.

representative_people.context: German conceptual history; not a branch of the Cambridge School. Separates words from concepts, concepts from social reality and analytical categories from historical actors’ vocabulary; experience and expectation organize questions rather than determine their answers.
representative_people.works: Vergangene Zukunft (1979); Futures Past (1985)

before.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.
strands.works: Philosophe, Philosophie, Handbuch Heft 3 (1985), pp. 7–14

strands.focus: Goldman distinguishes appeals to an enlightened general will from the divergent opinions of provinces. The meaning of public opinion changes within struggles over who can speak for a sovereign people.

before.relationship: Habermas’s public sphere connects political authority to public argument and communication
before.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Habermas distinguishes public discussion from state authority and ends with organizational accountability; Hohendahl records contemporary contestation. A conceptual resource, not proof all political historians adopted one model.

after.relationship: Habermas’s public sphere connects political authority to public argument and communication
after.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Habermas distinguishes public discussion from state authority and ends with organizational accountability; Hohendahl records contemporary contestation. A conceptual resource, not proof all political historians adopted one model. A specific Iberoamerican reception is now documented: Goldman (2000), 20, cites Guerra/Lempérière’s discussion of the Habermasian model while favoring plural public spaces; Sábato (2000), 257–259, appraises that adaptation and questions its conceptual and explanatory costs. Neither reading establishes universal adoption or a direct Habermas-to-Goldman textual genealogy beyond the cited mediation.

added.citation: Noemí Goldman, “Libertad de imprenta, opinión pública y debate constitucional en el Río de la Plata (1810–1827),” Prismas 4 (2000), 9–20.

verification.note: Complete primary article 9–20, including footnotes, read from institutional PDF. Follows press regulation, printers’ dependencies and competing claims to express public opinion during constitutional debate. Page 16 note 26 credits a 1997 joint presentation with Silvia Ratto; that presentation is not independently read or treated as coauthorship of the 2000 article. Page 20 invokes plural public spaces and cites Guerra/Lempérière on the Habermasian model. Original newspapers, assembly records and cited scholarship not independently audited; selected Rio de la Plata case, not all Latin America. Journal and repository differ on issue numbering; citation uses volume 4.

added.citation: Hilda Sábato, review of Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica, Prismas 4 (2000), 257–259.

verification.note: Complete primary review 257–259 read from institutional PDF with columns read in order. Appreciative and critical reception: identifies the collection’s Habermasian starting point, questions loss of conceptual specificity through concrete plural spaces, distinguishes cultural from structural explanation, and asks about republicanism and neglected contrasts. Statements about the 1998 introduction and chapters remain mediated through this review; neither whole collection nor its underlying archives read. Original scan spells Lempérière inconsistently; publisher metadata used for shared identity.

added.citation: François-Xavier Guerra and Annick Lempérière et al., Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica: Ambigüedades y problemas. Siglos XVIII–XIX (CEMCA/Fondo de Cultura Económica, 1998).

outcomes.finding: Goldman’s complete Rio de la Plata study supplies a specific political-history case connecting printing institutions, press freedom, contested public opinion and provincial sovereignty. Her explicit reference to plural public spaces and Sábato’s contemporary critical review document a concrete Iberoamerican adaptation of Habermas, including disagreement over the conceptual and explanatory costs. Named prior collaboration with Ratto and the Guerra/Lempérière collection establish research context without inventing a uniform school.
outcomes.research_limit: Goldman 9–20 and Sábato 257–259 fully read from institutional PDFs. Original newspapers, assembly records, the 1997 Goldman/Ratto presentation and the 1998 collection’s introduction/chapters unread. Publisher metadata confirms the latter’s identity only. Sábato’s account of the collection is mediated reception evidence. Regional case does not exhaust Latin America; no direct Skinner/Pocock lineage inferred, and inherited links retain their prior limits.
